judgments.forked_readings_summary:
All four readings describe the same task with essentially no semantic divergence. They unanimously agree on: TRIGGER (order status transition into SHIPPED, and only that transition — not other statuses), ACTION (send exactly one "order-shipped" email), CHANNEL (existing SendGrid client, reused as-is, not modified or swapped), RECIPIENT (order's billing email), DISPATCH (async/fire-and-forget, never blocks or fails the status-update request), and GUARD (persisted per-transition idempotency marker so it can never send twice). The in-scope surfaces match across all four: status-transition path as the hook-point, existing SendGrid client, an async dispatch mechanism, and a persisted idempotency record. The out-of-scope lists are nearly identical: SMS/push/in-app channels, notification-preferences UI, emails for any other status, template authoring, SendGrid client internals/provider swap, retry/dead-letter infra, and any blocking/failing/rolling-back of the request.

Two non-load-bearing nuances, neither a fork: (1) Reading 1 adds a meta-observation that this code-forge repo is the preflight framework source containing no order/SendGrid code, so it frames the deliverable as a "pinned behavior-spec/scope-guard artifact" for a downstream consumer rather than directly-edited application code — but it commits to the exact same behavioral boundary. This is a framing of WHERE the work lands, not WHAT the task is. (2) Readings 3 and 4 explicitly pin the hook to the POST-COMMIT point (after the status change persists), while Readings 1 and 2 leave the exact placement slightly looser ("observe the transition" / "background task"); this is a refinement of the same mechanism. Readings 1 and 3 also list tests as an explicit in-scope surface while 2 and 4 don't enumerate them — a detail-level rather than scope difference. The readings describe the same task.

All four readings describe the same task with no material divergence. Core behavior is identical across all four: on an order's status transition INTO SHIPPED, asynchronously (fire-and-forget) send exactly one 'order-shipped' SendGrid email (via the existing client) to the order's billing email, guarded by a persisted per-transition idempotency marker so it never sends twice and never blocks/fails the status-update request. Scope boundary is identical: one channel (email), one trigger (the SHIPPED transition only), one template, off the request's critical path. Out-of-scope lists are essentially the same across all four: SMS/push/in-app channels, notification-preferences UI, emails for any other status, SendGrid client changes/provider swaps, authoring the template content, and retry/dead-letter machinery beyond plain fire-and-forget. The only differences are minor elaboration, not semantic forks: (1) Reading 1 adds a meta-framing note that this code-forge repo is the preflight framework SOURCE and contains no order/SendGrid application code, so the deliverable would be a pinned behavior-spec/scope-guard artifact rather than editable order-service code — a context observation about WHERE the work lands, not a different reading of WHAT the task is. (2) Readings 1 and 3 explicitly list tests (send-on-SHIPPED, no-send on others, non-blocking, exactly-once) as in-scope surfaces; readings 2 and 4 don't enumerate tests but their behavior descriptions imply the same guarantees — a verbosity difference, not a scope conflict. (3) Readings 3 and 4 are slightly more precise about hooking the POST-COMMIT point and detecting non-SHIPPED to SHIPPED specifically, but this is the same trigger the other two describe in less detail. No reading adds or drops a channel, trigger, recipient, or template relative to the others.

All four readings describe the SAME task with essentially identical scope, surfaces, and behavior. Core behavior (unanimous): on an order's status transition INTO SHIPPED, asynchronously (fire-and-forget) send exactly one 'order-shipped' email via the EXISTING SendGrid client to the order's billing email, guarded by a persisted per-transition idempotency marker so it never sends twice and never blocks/fails the status-update request.

Scope boundary (unanimous): the boundary stops hard at this one channel (email), one trigger (the →SHIPPED transition only), one template, with no impact on the request's critical path/latency/transaction.

Surfaces in-scope (unanimous): (1) the order status-transition code path as the trigger/hook point, (2) the existing SendGrid client called with the 'order-shipped' template + billing email, (3) an async/queued/background dispatch so the send is non-blocking, (4) a persistence-backed idempotency record keyed to the order+SHIPPED transition. Three of four also explicitly list tests (send-on-SHIPPED, no-send on other transitions, exactly-once, non-blocking) — but listing tests vs. omitting them is a detail-level difference, not a scope fork; all four imply the same exactly-once / non-blocking behavior must hold.

Surfaces out-of-scope (unanimous): SMS/push/in-app channels, notification-preferences UI / opt-in-out, emails for any other status, editing the SendGrid template content, changing/swapping the SendGrid client, retry/dead-letter/observability beyond plain fire-and-forget, blocking/failing/rolling back the status update on send error, and recipient logic beyond billing email.

Trivial, non-material variations only:
- Reading #1 alone adds a meta-note that this code-forge repo is the preflight FRAMEWORK source (no order/SendGrid app code exists in-repo), so the deliverable is the pinned behavior-spec/scope-guard artifact for a downstream consumer rather than literal order-service edits. The others write as if editing real order code. This is a framing/context difference about WHERE the work lands, not a difference in what behavior is being specified — the contract being captured is byte-for-byte the same. Worth flagging but not a fork.
- #3 and #4 explicitly anchor the hook at the POST-COMMIT point and #3 specifies the transition predicate (old != SHIPPED && new == SHIPPED); #1/#2 say 'on transition into SHIPPED' without naming post-commit. Same intent (detect the entry into SHIPPED, after the status persists), just stated at different precision.

No axis forks. Differences are detail/framing only.
